question: How does the text describe Job at the beginning (his character, his family, his possessions), and what did he do after his sons' feasts?
Satan asks whether Job fears God “for nothing”: what suspicion does this question raise about Job's faith and about faith in general?
The verb בָרַךְ (barakh, “bless”) appears in verses 5, 10 and 21, sometimes translated as “curse”: why can the same verb carry such opposite meanings in these verses?
Job worships and says “the LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away”: what place does worship have for you when you lose something important?
What changes in the second test compared with the first, and how do Job and his wife react?
God says Satan incited Him against Job “without cause”: how does this expression prepare the reader for the debates to come?
The verb חָזַק (chazaq, “hold fast”) appears in God's words (v. 3) and in those of Job's wife (v. 9): what meaning does the idea of holding on to integrity take in each mouth?
The friends stay silent for seven days before Job's pain: what can this silence teach you about being near someone who suffers?
In Job's first speech, what day and what night does he curse, and what images of light and darkness does he use for it?
Why does Job imagine death as a place of rest where kings, prisoners and slaves are together?
The verb נוּחַ (nuach, “rest”) appears in verses 13, 17 and 26: how does the search for rest run through Job's lament?
Job does not hide his despair when he asks “why is light given to the miserable”: what room is there in your faith for prayers of honest lament?
In the first speech of Eliphaz the Temanite, what memory does he bring up from Job's past, and what question does he ask about his confidence and hope?
Eliphaz asks “who, being innocent, has ever perished?”: what idea about suffering and guilt lies behind this question?
The word רוּחַ (ruach, “wind, breath, spirit”) appears in verse 9 and verse 15: what role does it have in the night vision Eliphaz reports?
Eliphaz begins with gentle words before correcting Job: how do you usually speak with someone who is suffering and whom you think is wrong?
Eliphaz goes on speaking: what actions of God does he list when he says “I would appeal to God”?
Eliphaz calls “blessed” the man whom God corrects: how does this idea help, and how can it wound someone in Job's situation?
The word עָמָל (amal, “trouble, toil”) appears in verses 6 and 7: where does Eliphaz say human suffering comes from, and how does the image of the sparks illustrate this?
Eliphaz ends with “we have examined this, and it is true”: when you speak with someone who suffers, how much do you draw on your own experience and how much do you listen to theirs?
In Job's answer to Eliphaz, what images does he use to describe the weight of his pain and its source?
Why does Job compare his friends to streams that dry up in the heat and disappoint the caravans?
The verb בִּין (bin, “understand, discern”) appears in verses 24 and 30: what does Job ask of his friends and what does he claim about himself with this verb?
Job says that friends should show kindness to the despairing: what kind of friend have you been to someone in crisis?
What comparisons does Job use to describe his days and his nights in verses 1 to 6?
The words “what is man that You should exalt him” recall Psalm 8: what meaning do they take in Job's mouth?
The verb שׁוּב (shuv, “return”) appears in verses 7 and 10: what does Job say will not return, and what view of death does this reveal?
Job decides: “I will not restrain my mouth”: what have you been keeping back, without the courage to say it to God?
In the first speech of Bildad the Shuhite, how does he explain the death of Job's children, and what does he promise if Job seeks God?
Bildad says to ask “the former generation”: what value and what limit does wisdom inherited from the ancients have for understanding Job's case?
The verb עָוַת (avat, “pervert”) appears twice in verse 3: what conviction about God's justice does Bildad defend with this question?
Bildad speaks of hopes as fragile as a spider's web: on what have you been resting your security?
In Job's answer to Bildad, what works of God in creation does he describe, and in what tone?
Job laments that there is no “mediator” between him and God: what does this desire reveal about his situation?
The verb צָדַק (tsadaq, “be righteous”) appears in verses 2, 15 and 20: what question about human righteousness before God does Job raise with it?
Job says he cannot simply smile and forget his complaint: how do you deal with the pressure to seem fine when you are not?
Job continues his answer to Bildad, now speaking directly to God: how does he describe the way God formed him in verses 8 to 12?
Why does Job ask whether God has “eyes of flesh” and sees as a human being sees?
The word צַלְמָוֶת (tsalmavet, “shadow of death”) appears in verses 21 and 22: how does Job describe the place where he thinks he is going?
Job asks God “let me know why You prosecute me”: have you ever asked a question like this, and what did you do with the silence that may have followed?
In the first speech of Zophar the Naamathite, what does he accuse Job of, and what does he say about the punishment Job deserves?
Zophar speaks of God's wisdom, higher than the heavens and deeper than Sheol: is this truth used here to comfort Job or to silence him?
The verb מָצָא (matsa, “find, attain”) lies behind “fathom” in verse 7: what does Zophar say human beings cannot attain?
Zophar promises light and security if Job repents: when have you heard or given a simple recipe for a complicated suffering?
In Job's answer to Zophar, whom does he tell them to ask about the hand of the LORD, and what would these creatures teach?
In what tone does Job say “wisdom will die with you,” and what does this irony show about the conversation so far?
The word חׇכְמָה (chokhmah, “wisdom”) appears in verses 2, 12 and 13: where does Job say it is, and how does this contrast with the friends' wisdom?
Job observes that those at ease look down on another's misfortune: in what situation might your comfort have made you less sensitive to someone's pain?
What does Job accuse his friends of in verses 4 to 12, and what names does he give them and their defenses?
Job asks whether his friends will “speak wickedly on God's behalf”: what does it mean to defend God unjustly?
The verb יָכַח (yakhach, “argue, plead a case”) appears in verses 3, 10 and 15: before whom does Job want to present his case, and with what attitude?
Job says “though He slay me, I will hope in Him; I will surely defend my ways”: how can trust and complaint live together in your prayer?
What images does Job use at the beginning of the chapter to describe the life of man “born of woman”?
Job compares man to a tree cut down that sprouts again and asks “if a man dies, will he live again?”: what hope does he seem to look for and not find?
The word תִּקְוָה (tiqvah, “hope”) appears in verse 7 and verse 19: what happens to hope between one verse and the other?
Job says human days “are determined”: how does the awareness that life is short affect your choices today?
In Eliphaz's second speech, what questions does he ask to show that Job is no wiser than the others?
Eliphaz describes at length the fate of the wicked: why does he choose this portrait now, and to whom might Job feel compared?
The verb אָמַן (aman, “trust, believe”) appears in verses 15, 22 and 31: who trusts, who does not believe, and in what, according to Eliphaz?
Eliphaz asks whether “the consolations of God” are not enough for Job: when can correct religious words sound harsh to someone who suffers?
In Job's answer to Eliphaz, with what images of attack does he describe what God has done to him?
Job, who feels attacked by God, says his “witness is in heaven”: how should we understand this tension within the same speech?
The verb נָחַם (nacham, “comfort”) gives rise to the “miserable comforters” of verse 2: what did Job expect from those who came to comfort him, according to verses 4 and 5?
Job says that in his friends' place he would use his mouth to bring relief: what words of yours could bring relief to someone this week?
Job goes on speaking: with whom does he claim kinship in verses 13 and 14, and what questions does he ask about his hope?
Job asks God for “a pledge” and asks who will shake hands with him: what does this request show about how he sees God at that moment?
The word שְׁאוֹל (she’ol, “Sheol”) appears in verses 13 and 16: what images does Job associate with this place of the dead?
Even crushed, Job affirms that “the righteous will hold to his way”: what helps you keep going when you see no way out?
In Bildad's second speech, what images of a light put out and of traps does he use for the wicked?
Bildad speaks of a memory wiped out and of having neither son nor grandson: knowing what Job lost in chapter 1, what effect would these words have on him?
The word בַּלָּהָה (ballahah, “terror”) appears in verses 11 and 14, culminating in the “king of terrors”: what figure does Bildad seem to describe?
Bildad complains of being regarded as stupid and wants to be heard: when a hard conversation turns into a dispute for you, what changes its course?
In Job's answer to Bildad, who has turned away from him, and how does each group treat him now?
Why does Job wish his words were engraved in rock, and what does he hope to see “in my flesh”?
The word גֹּאֵל (go’el, “kinsman-redeemer, Redeemer”) appears in verse 25: what function did this relative have in Israel, and what does it mean for Job to say “my Redeemer lives”?
Job pleads “have pity on me, my friends”: who near you may be asking for compassion without being heard?
In Zophar's second speech, what images does he use to show how brief the joy of the wicked is?
Zophar describes evil as something sweet in the mouth that turns to venom in the stomach: what does this image say about the nature of sin, and does it really apply to Job?
The verb בָּלַע (bala‘, “swallow”) appears in verses 15 and 18: what happens to the riches the wicked swallowed, according to Zophar?
Zophar condemns whoever “has oppressed and forsaken the poor”: in what way is this denunciation still valid even if his reasoning about Job is wrong?
In Job's answer to Zophar, how does he describe the life of the wicked, of their children and of their goods?
Job compares two men who die, one prosperous and the other bitter, who “lie down together in the dust”: what argument of the friends is he contesting?
The word רָשָׁע (rasha‘, “wicked”) appears in verses 7, 16 and 17: how does Job use the experience of the wicked to answer his friends?
Job calls his friends' answers comfort “in vain”: when you realize a ready-made answer does not solve anything, what do you do next?
In Eliphaz's third speech, of what concrete sins does he accuse Job?
Eliphaz asks whether human righteousness is “of benefit to the Almighty”: what image of God appears behind this question?
The verb שָׁלַם (shalam, “be at peace, pay”) appears in verses 21 and 27: what relationship does Eliphaz draw between being reconciled with God and fulfilling vows?
The invitation “submit to God and be at peace with Him” can be good in itself and still be badly applied: how do you tell good advice from the right advice for the right person?
In Job's answer to Eliphaz, in which directions does he look for God, and what does he find?
Job says “when He has tested me, I will come forth as gold”: how does this confidence fit with the feeling that God is absent?
The verb יָדַע (yada‘, “know”) appears in verses 3, 5 and 10: what would Job like to know, and what does he affirm that God knows?
Job sighs “if only I knew where to find Him”: what paths do you take when God seems distant?
Job goes on: what injustices against orphans, widows and the poor does he describe in verses 2 to 12?
Job asks why the Almighty does not set “times” of judgment: what problem does he raise about justice in the world?
The word אַלְמָנָה (almanah, “widow”) appears in verses 3 and 21: what place does the widow have in the law and the prophets of Israel, and what does her mention here denounce?
The text says “the souls of the wounded cry out”: what cries of vulnerable people around you do you tend not to hear?
Bildad's third speech is the shortest of all: what ideas about God and about the human being does he repeat in only six verses?
The question “how can a man be righteous before God?” has already appeared in Job's mouth (9:2): what difference does it make who asks it and with what intention?
The word שָׁלוֹם (shalom, “peace”) appears in verse 2: what kind of peace does Bildad attribute to God “in His heights,” and how does it contrast with Job's situation?
Bildad calls the human being a “maggot” and a “worm”: how do you balance humility before God with the value the Bible gives to the human person?
In Job's answer to Bildad, what works of God over the waters, the sky and Sheol does he describe?
After so many wonders, Job says these are “but the fringes of His ways”: what does this phrase suggest about the limits of what we know of God?
The word נְשָׁמָה (neshamah, “breath, spirit”) appears in verse 4: what question does Job ask Bildad about the origin of his words?
Job mocks the help he received from his friends: how can you know whether your help really strengthens someone who is weak?
Job resumes his discourse with an oath: what does he swear about his lips, his integrity and his righteousness?
Verses 13 to 23 describe the end of the wicked in words similar to the friends', and some readers think this part belongs to another speaker: how should we understand these verses in Job's mouth?
The verb סוּר (sur, “take away, remove”) appears in verses 2 and 5: what does Job say God has taken from him, and what does he refuse to take away from himself?
Job says “I will hold fast my righteousness”: in what situation did keeping a clear conscience cost you something?
What human work of mining and searching for treasure does the poem describe in verses 1 to 11?
This poem about wisdom interrupts the debate, and it is not clear whether Job or a narrator's voice is speaking: what role does it play at this point in the book?
The word חׇכְמָה (chokhmah, “wisdom”) appears in verses 12, 18, 20 and 28: what path does the poem take to arrive at the definition of verse 28?
The poem ends with “the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom”: what concrete form can this fear take in your daily life?
Job continues his final speech recalling the past: what did he do for the poor, the orphan, the widow, the blind and the lame?
Job remembers the days when “God's friendship rested on my tent”: what does he miss most, his goods or his relationship with God?
The word סוֹד (sod, “intimate counsel, friendship”) appears in verse 4: what kind of closeness to God does this word suggest?
Job says “I was eyes to the blind and feet to the lame”: for whom could you be eyes or feet today?
Job continues his final speech contrasting the past with the “now”: who mocks him, and how are these people described?
Job says to God “I cry out to You, but You do not answer”: how did this silence of God become the center of his pain?
The verb שָׁוַע (shava‘, “cry for help”) appears in verses 20 and 28: to whom does Job cry, and what answer does he receive in each case?
Job remembers that he wept for those in trouble: how has your own suffering changed the way you look at the pain of others?
What areas of life does Job examine in his oath of innocence in verses 1 to 12?
Job justifies fair treatment of the servant by saying the same God formed them both in the womb: what view of human dignity appears here?
The word בְּרִית (berit, “covenant”) appears in verse 1: what does it mean for Job to make a covenant “with my eyes”?
Job denies having said to gold “you are my security”: what, in practice, takes the place of security in your life?
Who is Elihu, how does the narrator introduce him, and why does he become angry with Job and with the three friends?
Elihu waited to speak because he was young, but says wisdom comes from “the spirit in a man”: what does he question in the idea that age guarantees wisdom?
The verb חָרָה (charah, “burn with anger”) appears in verses 2, 3 and 5: against whom does Elihu's anger burn, and why?
Elihu says he is “full of words,” like wineskins about to burst: how do you tell the urge to speak from the real need to be heard?
Elihu addresses Job by name: which of Job's words does he quote, and how does he summarize them?
Elihu says God speaks “once, even twice,” through dreams and warnings: how does this idea answer Job's complaint that God does not answer?
The word שַׁחַת (shachat, “pit”) appears five times in the chapter: from what does God want to deliver the human soul, according to Elihu?
Elihu imagines a “mediator, one out of a thousand” who intercedes for the sufferer: who has been this kind of mediator for you, or for whom could you be one?
In Elihu's second speech, what sentences does he attribute to Job, and how does he evaluate them?
Elihu insists that “God does no wrong” and that all life depends on His breath: in what does he agree with the three friends, and in what does he seem to go further?
The word מִשְׁפָּט (mishpat, “justice, right”) appears in verses 4, 12, 17 and 23: what question about God's justice does Elihu want to settle?
Elihu proposes the prayer “teach me what I cannot see”: what blind spots would you like God to show you in yourself?
In Elihu's third speech, what does he say Job's sin or righteousness can or cannot do to God and to others?
Elihu observes that the oppressed cry out, but “no one says, ‘Where is God my Maker’”: what difference does he see between crying out in pain and seeking God?
The verb נָבַט (navat, “look carefully”) opens verse 5: what does Elihu tell Job to contemplate, and what lesson does he want to draw from it?
Elihu speaks of the God “who gives songs in the night”: what song, prayer or word has sustained you on a hard night?
Elihu goes on: according to verses 8 to 12, what does God do with those bound in affliction, and what two paths open from there?
Elihu says God “opens their ears in oppression”: how does this view of suffering as teaching differ from the view of the three friends?
The verb גָּלָה (galah, “reveal, uncover”) appears in verses 10 and 15: what does God reveal, and in what circumstance, according to Elihu?
Elihu invites Job to extol God's work, even without understanding Him: what place does praise have when you do not understand what is happening?
Elihu ends his speeches by describing the storm: what natural phenomena does he attribute to God's voice?
Elihu asks Job whether he knows the wonders of the clouds and the sky: how do these questions anticipate God's speech in the next chapter?
The verb פָּלָא (pala’, “be wonderful”) appears in verses 5 and 14: what does it mean to call God's works “wonders” in a book that discusses His justice?
Elihu says “stop and consider the wonders of God”: when was the last time you stopped to contemplate creation?
When the LORD finally speaks to Job, what questions does He ask about the foundation of the earth and the limits of the sea?
God does not explain to Job why he suffered, but asks questions: what does this way of answering suggest about the relationship between the two?
The word סַעַר (sa‘ar, “storm, whirlwind”) appears in verse 1: what does it mean for God to answer Job “out of the whirlwind,” after so many human speeches?
God speaks of the One who provides food for the lion and for the raven's young: what does this image say to you about your worries today?
What wild animals does God present to Job in verses 1 to 18, and what do they have in common with regard to human beings?
Why does God include the ostrich, which seems “deprived of wisdom,” in this parade of creation?
The verb שָׂחַק (sachaq, “laugh, scorn”) appears in verses 7, 18 and 22: what do the wild donkey, the ostrich and the horse laugh at, and what does this show about their freedom?
The creation God describes is beautiful and also wild: how do you live with the idea of a world that does not revolve around you?
Between the two speeches of the LORD, Job speaks briefly: what does he say, and what gesture does he make?
God asks “would you condemn Me to justify yourself?”: what balance between God's justice and Job's innocence does this question put at stake?
The word גֵּאֶה (ge’eh, “proud”) appears in verses 11 and 12: what does God challenge Job to do with the proud, and what does this challenge reveal?
Job puts his hand over his mouth and decides not to go on: in what situation would silence before God be a more honest answer for you than words?
What questions does the LORD ask Job about Leviathan in verses 1 to 11, and what kind of relationship with human beings do they rule out?
After speaking of Leviathan, God says “who then can stand against Me?” and “everything under heaven is Mine”: what link is there between the untamable creature and the Creator?
The word לִוְיָתָן (livyatan, “Leviathan”) appears in verse 1: what images does this name evoke in other biblical texts, and why does it appear at the end of the book?
Leviathan is described as something no human being can master: what in your life do you need to recognize is out of your control?
After the speeches, what does the LORD say to Eliphaz and his two friends, and what role does Job receive on their behalf?
Job says “my ears had heard of You, but now my eyes have seen You”: what has changed in his relationship with God, if the questions about suffering were not answered?
The verb נָחַם (nacham) appears in verse 6 (“I repent”) and in verse 11 (“comforted him”): how does this same word link Job's change to the comfort he finally receives?
Job is restored “after he had prayed for his friends,” the same ones who wounded him with words: for whom could you pray even without having received an apology?
